Chapter Six: The Trap of Utility and the Loss of Wonder
Ever notice how easy it is to slip right back into your old routines? That’s exactly what happens to our friend here. Just a few weeks after his experiment, he’s swept up again in errands, deadlines, and the buzz of everyday life. All that color and meaning he’d found—suddenly, it starts to fade. Flowers on the table? They’re just flowers now. The sky? It’s just a backdrop for another busy day.
He can actually feel his mind pulling him back into old habits. The practical stuff takes over, and the world feels a little flatter, less alive.
One day, he watches a friend working away, barely glancing outside. It hits him—there’s this numbness that settles in when life becomes something we just manage, not something we marvel at.
Most of us, he realizes, get trapped by the need to be useful. We measure our days by what we accomplish, by what we can count or explain. The world starts to feel like a tool—nothing more than a means to an end.
But then, something unexpected happens. Maybe it’s a shaft of sunlight, a child’s laughter, or just the fresh scent of rain on pavement. These little moments shake him awake, even if it’s just for a heartbeat. Suddenly, the world feels new again. He remembers that feeling—how everything seemed alive, deeply connected.
That’s when he realizes: wonder is always there, waiting. But it takes a conscious choice. You have to pause, really look, and—most of all—let go of this constant need to be useful.
He thinks about a teacher he knows. At the end of a long, exhausting day, she simply stops to watch the sunset. For a little while, all the worries and to-do lists just fall away. The colors in the sky? They’re enough. She doesn’t need to explain them or do anything with them—they just are. And in that moment, she feels a quiet joy, a sense of belonging to something bigger.
Our friend starts to see the real challenge isn’t chasing after extraordinary experiences. It’s about finding wonder right in the middle of the ordinary. The doors of perception—they aren’t locked. Most people just don’t notice them. But the world? It’s always ready to offer invitations to see more deeply, if we’re paying attention.
So he makes a promise to himself: to stay alert for those moments when the world quietly reveals itself. It’s not about escaping from life—it’s about being fully present for it.
Sure, the trap of utility is strong. But with a little willingness to wonder, it starts to loosen. And maybe, just maybe, that’s where the real magic of being alive begins.
